analysis.one_liner: Forces Medicare patients' malpractice claims into binding arbitration with capped damages.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by one House Republican and two cosponsors, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have automatically forced every malpractice claim by a Medicare patient into binding arbitration instead of court — patients would be deemed to have agreed to arbitrate whether they wanted to or not. Panels of three arbitrators would decide both fault and compensation, with noneconomic damages capped at $250,000, awards reduced by any money collected from other sources like health insurance, large awards paid in installments, and lawyers' contingency fees capped on a sliding scale. Appeals to state court would be allowed only on narrow grounds like fraud or panel misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers would gain the most. Every Medicare malpractice claim would be decided by an arbitrator rather than a jury, noneconomic damages would be capped at $250,000 (or the state's lower cap), awards would be reduced by collateral-source payments, and payouts over $100,000 would be paid in installments. Claims would also move faster, with discovery limited to six months and decisions due roughly 90 days later. Some patients with clear-cut claims might get paid quicker and with less legal expense, but the structural winners are the providers and insurers whose payouts shrink.

how_it_helps.text: Would remove malpractice cases involving Medicare patients from juries entirely: every beneficiary and provider would be 'deemed to have entered into an agreement to arbitrate' any malpractice claim, with no way to opt out.

Would cap noneconomic damages at $250,000 (or the state's limit if lower), reduce awards by any collateral-source money the patient collected, pay awards over $100,000 in installments, and cap lawyers' contingency fees at 25/15/10 percent tiers — all of which directly limits what providers and their insurers pay out.
Would speed up resolution: discovery must begin within 20 days and finish within 6 months, with a decision due about 90 days later, instead of a court case that can drag on for years.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare patients injured by negligent care. They would lose the right to a jury trial without ever consenting, face a hard $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages like pain and suffering, see awards reduced dollar-for-dollar by insurance or disability payments from other sources, and have only narrow grounds to appeal an arbitrator's decision to state court. Capped attorney fees could also make lawyers less willing to take harder cases, and claims would have to be filed within two years of discovering the injury. The system itself would be paid for out of the Medicare trust funds.

drawbacks.text: The arbitration would be mandatory and imposed: beneficiaries would be 'deemed' to have agreed to arbitrate every malpractice claim arising from Medicare-covered care, giving up their right to a jury trial without any actual consent.

Compensation would shrink for the most seriously injured: noneconomic damages capped at $250,000, awards reduced by any collateral-source payments (so a patient whose health insurer paid the medical bills recovers less), and no wrongful-death claims by survivors allowed at all.

The sliding-scale cap on contingency fees and the short two-year filing window would make it harder for injured patients to find a lawyer and to bring a claim at all, especially for injuries that surface slowly.

The bill's defenders argued — and the design reflects — that malpractice suits were slow and costly, and that arbitration panels with strict deadlines, public hearings, and subpoena power could resolve valid claims faster and cheaper for both sides; patients with clear-cut injuries might indeed be paid sooner.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real efficiencies — faster decisions, guaranteed process, subpoena power, public hearings, and proportionate fault reduction instead of all-or-nothing verdicts. But those benefits are secondary: the core exchange was that doctors, hospitals, and insurers would pay out less, and the money saved would come directly out of the pockets of injured seniors through the $250,000 noneconomic cap, collateral-source offsets, installment payments, and fee caps that shrink legal representation. A patient can sue faster, but recover much less, with no jury and almost no appeal. For ordinary Medicare beneficiaries, the costs plainly outweighed the convenience.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees in April 1990, and no one ever scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress went out of session in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Nancy Johnson of Connecticut introduced the bill on April 19, 1990, with two Republican cosponsors.

It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees — the two panels that share jurisdiction over Medicare — which referred it to their health subcommittees on April 26 and 27, 1990.
No hearing, markup, vote, or report ever followed; the last recorded action is the subcommittee referrals, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries are better off: they kept the right to take malpractice claims to court before a jury, with no $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages and no collateral-source offsets. Doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers got none of the liability relief the bill would have handed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare patients, who kept full court rights

for.name: Nancy L. Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 19, 1990, proposing mandatory binding arbitration for all Medicare malpractice claims.

for.name: 2 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members of either party signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Dan Rostenkowski)
against.role: Committee of primary referral for Medicare legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on April 26, 1990, and never scheduled a markup or vote; the committee took no further action.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair John Dingell)
against.role: Committee of joint referral for health legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee on April 27, 1990, and never scheduled a markup or vote; the committee took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all three sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committees with jurisdiction never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would remove all Medicare malpractice claims from juries and cap noneconomic damages at $250,000, offset collateral-source payments, and pay large awards in installments — sharply reducing what providers owe seniors harmed by negligent care. Their gain comes directly out of injured patients' recoveries.
Binding arbitration, damage caps, and strict deadlines would make payouts smaller and more predictable, cutting the industry's claim costs on behalf of Medicare-covered care.

The bill would create a permanent, federally funded 'Medical Services Dispute Resolution Organization' in every state, paid from the Medicare trust funds, to administer all Medicare malpractice arbitrations — locking in a new industry's gatekeeper role over patients' injury claims.

Sliding-scale contingency fee caps and mandatory arbitration would cut both the fees and the volume of malpractice work, leaving injured patients with thinner legal representation — in this bill the lawyers' loss and the patients' loss are the same loss.
